# security.txt standards baseline

Research date: 2026-03-10

## Executive baseline

The current security.txt standard is [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html), which obsoletes RFC 2142's narrower treatment of a security contact. For an HTTP service, the interoperable baseline is a UTF-8 plain-text document at `https://<authority>/.well-known/security.txt` containing one or more `Contact` fields and exactly one unexpired `Expires` field. The standard makes all other currently registered fields optional. Product behavior should be based on RFC 9116 and the live [IANA Security.txt Fields registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/security-txt-fields/security-txt-fields.xhtml), not on which controls happen to appear in the securitytxt.org generator.

Normative words below describe RFC requirements only where the RFC uses them. Generator behavior is called out separately as convenience behavior.

## 1. Syntax, fields, and multiplicity

RFC 9116 defines a line-oriented format. A field line consists of a registered field name, `:`, one space, and its value; field names use letters, digits, and hyphens. Field names are case-insensitive, while values retain the semantics of their field. Blank lines and comment lines are also allowed. URI-valued fields use URI syntax; `Preferred-Languages` is a comma-separated list of language tags; `Expires` is an RFC 3339 date-time constrained as described below. See [RFC 9116 §3 and its ABNF](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3), [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html), [RFC 5646](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5646.html), and [RFC 3339 §5.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html#section-5.6).

The current standard fields are:

| Field | Required? | Multiplicity | Normative meaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `Contact` | **Required** | One or more | A URI describing how to report a vulnerability. Multiple contact methods may be published. Common schemes include `mailto:` and `https:`; accepting a URI is not the same as proving that the destination works. [RFC 9116 §2.5.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.3) |
| `Expires` | **Required** | Exactly one | UTC RFC 3339 date-time after which the file is stale and must not be treated as current. [RFC 9116 §2.5.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.5) |
| `Acknowledgments` | Optional | Zero or more | URI of a page recognizing security researchers. [RFC 9116 §2.5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.1) |
| `Canonical` | Optional unless clear-signed | Zero or more | URI identifying a canonical location of this same file; when the file is digitally signed, at least one `Canonical` field is required and must match the retrieval URI. [RFC 9116 §2.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.2) |
| `Encryption` | Optional | Zero or more | URI pointing to encryption keys or other information for encrypted communication. It is not itself an inline key. [RFC 9116 §2.5.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.4) |
| `Hiring` | Optional | Zero or more | URI for security-related job openings. [RFC 9116 §2.5.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.6) |
| `Policy` | Optional | Zero or more | URI of the service's security/disclosure policy. [RFC 9116 §2.5.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.7) |
| `Preferred-Languages` | Optional | At most one | One or more comma-separated BCP 47 language tags, in descending order of preference. [RFC 9116 §2.5.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.8) |

The registry is extensible. Consumers must ignore fields they do not recognize, and new standardized field names are added through the IANA registration policy rather than by silently assigning new semantics to an existing name. A control panel therefore should preserve or deliberately expose unknown extension lines if round-tripping is a goal; rejecting every unknown field would impair forward compatibility. See [RFC 9116 §3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3.1) and the live [IANA registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/security-txt-fields/security-txt-fields.xhtml).

### Expiry

`Expires` must represent a date and time in UTC using the RFC 3339 Internet date/time profile. RFC 9116 recommends a value less than one year into the future. A client must not use a file after its `Expires` time. This is document freshness, independent of HTTP cache freshness; both need to be honored. [RFC 9116 §2.5.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.5)

### Canonical

`Canonical` is not generally mandatory for an unsigned file. It becomes mandatory for a digitally signed file, where at least one value must match the URI used to retrieve that file. Multiple values allow the same content to identify more than one canonical deployment URI. This makes an automatically inferred value a product convenience, not a universal RFC default: virtual hosting, alternate ports, proxy headers, IDNs, and multi-site publication can make inference wrong. [RFC 9116 §2.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.2) and [§3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3)

### Comments and ordering

A comment line begins with `#`; comments and blank lines are permitted and do not define fields. Field order is not semantically significant. RFC 9116 gives a recommended human-readable ordering, but parsers cannot depend on it, and generators need not reorder user-authored content merely to be valid. Duplicate fields are valid only according to each field's multiplicity rules. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3)

## 2. HTTP discovery and representation

### Endpoint discovery

For an HTTP service, the standard location is the well-known URI `/.well-known/security.txt` on the authority being queried, and retrieval must use HTTPS. The legacy top-level `/security.txt` location may additionally be served for compatibility, but it is not a substitute for the well-known location. Well-known URI processing is governed by [RFC 8615](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615.html); security.txt's concrete discovery requirements are in [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3).

Scope follows the origin/authority being queried; a file found on one hostname should not silently be treated as authorization for unrelated hosts. The `Canonical` field identifies copies but does not turn arbitrary cross-origin content into an authoritative policy for every host. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3) and the origin model in [RFC 6454](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6454.html)

### Media type, charset, and line endings

The response media type is `text/plain` and the charset is UTF-8; the interoperable response header is `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`. Producers must emit valid UTF-8. Lines may end in either LF or CRLF under the security.txt grammar. A generated unsigned file should choose one style consistently; CRLF deserves special attention when OpenPGP cleartext signing because that framework canonicalizes line endings. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3), [`text/plain` in RFC 2046 §4.1.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2046.html#section-4.1.3), and [RFC 4880 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7)

### Status and redirects

Successful discovery is an HTTP `200 (OK)` representation at the well-known endpoint (possibly reached through a redirect). RFC 9116 clients are expected to handle redirects, but the RFC places security limits on redirect processing, including HTTPS destinations and a bounded redirect chain. A control panel should not assume that publishing a `3xx`, authentication challenge, HTML error page, or `200` fallback page containing non-security.txt content is equivalent to publishing a valid file. The current definitions of status-code and redirect semantics are in [RFC 9110 §§15.3.1 and 15.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.3.1), with security.txt-specific retrieval behavior in [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3).

Compatibility implication: serving the bytes directly at the well-known path is the least surprising baseline. If redirects are supported, the owner must decide whether to permit only same-origin redirects or also RFC-permitted cross-origin HTTPS redirects, and must test the framework/publisher so redirect loops and HTTP downgrades cannot occur.

### Caching

HTTP cache directives apply normally, but a cached representation cannot remain semantically current beyond its `Expires` field. The publisher should set cache freshness so it ends no later than document expiry and should allow a promptly updated contact or policy to propagate. Conversely, the document's `Expires` value does not itself replace HTTP `Cache-Control` or HTTP cache validation. See [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3) and the current HTTP caching specification, [RFC 9111](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html).

A practical generator can compute `max-age <= Expires - now`, but that computation is convenience behavior, not a new security.txt field requirement. Product policy still has to address shared caches/CDNs, clock skew, revalidation (`ETag`/`Last-Modified`), emergency updates, and whether an expired configured document is served with warnings, rejected, or automatically disabled.

## 3. OpenPGP clear-signing

RFC 9116 permits, but does not require, the entire security.txt file to be digitally signed using the OpenPGP cleartext signature framework. This is a clear-signed document (`BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE`, `Hash` header, clear text, and armored signature), not an attached signature field and not merely an `Encryption` URI. When signed, `Canonical` is mandatory and at least one canonical URI must match the URI from which the signed file was retrieved. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3) and [RFC 4880 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7)

Cleartext signing has byte-level constraints: trailing spaces/tabs are ignored for signature calculation, line endings are canonicalized to CRLF for hashing, and lines beginning with a hyphen are dash-escaped in the armored cleartext form. Implementations should delegate this to a conforming OpenPGP library rather than reproduce it with ad hoc string transformations. [RFC 4880 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7)

RFC 4880 was obsoleted by the current OpenPGP specification, [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html), but RFC 9116's normative reference and deployed security.txt tooling use the cleartext-signature framework terminology established by RFC 4880. This creates an explicit compatibility decision: select library/key/signature profiles that satisfy current OpenPGP security guidance while remaining verifiable by deployed security.txt consumers. The product also needs a key custody and rotation model; RFC conformance alone does not make server-side storage of a private signing key safe. [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) and [RFC 9116 references](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#name-normative-references)

## 4. securitytxt.org authoring/generation inventory

[securitytxt.org](https://securitytxt.org/) is the first-party project site associated with the standard and exposes an interactive authoring generator. Its source repository is published as [`securitytxt/securitytxt.org`](https://github.com/securitytxt/securitytxt.org). These are useful UX references, not a second standards authority.

The site's authoring surface covers the registered baseline fields: required contact and expiry, plus acknowledgments, canonical location, encryption information, hiring, policy, and preferred languages. It guides a user through values and emits security.txt text suitable for copying/downloading. Any default expiry, field ordering, repeat/add controls, URI widgets, language picker, examples, or automatic formatting supplied by that UI are generator conveniences; validity and multiplicity remain controlled by RFC 9116 and IANA. See the live [generator](https://securitytxt.org/) and its [first-party source](https://github.com/securitytxt/securitytxt.org).

Not in scope here: the site's facility for validating an arbitrary remote site. This baseline inventories authoring/generation only and does not recommend proxying, reproducing, or depending on its remote validator.

A product should not infer from the site's UI that it may:

- omit either `Contact` or `Expires`;
- force optional fields to be present;
- reject registered future extensions merely because no widget exists;
- treat a default expiry interval as normative;
- assume generated output is deployed at the URL declared by `Canonical`;
- claim that a generated contact, URL, encryption key, or signature has been operationally verified; or
- call an unsigned generated file non-conforming, since signing is optional.

## 5. Concrete owner decisions

The following choices are not completely determined by the RFC and should be made explicitly before implementation:

1. **Authoring model (high product impact):** structured fields only, raw text only, or a hybrid. A structured-only model is simpler but needs a strategy for comments, blank lines, and unknown IANA extension fields to avoid lossy round trips.
2. **Multiplicity UX (medium):** repeatable controls for `Contact`, `Acknowledgments`, `Canonical`, `Encryption`, `Hiring`, and `Policy`; singleton enforcement for `Expires` and `Preferred-Languages`; and whether duplicate singletons are hard errors at save time.
3. **URI schemes (medium):** whether to accept every syntactically valid URI allowed by the RFC or constrain schemes for safety/UX. `mailto:` and HTTPS are important; a restrictive allowlist is a product policy and could exclude legitimate registered URI schemes.
4. **Expiry lifecycle (high):** default interval (while keeping it under the RFC's recommended one-year horizon), warning cadence, renewal flow, clock source, and behavior when configured content expires. Silent perpetual auto-extension undermines the purpose of explicit expiry.
5. **Canonical derivation (high):** manual values versus proxy-aware inference; behavior across virtual hosts, sites, ports, aliases, and alternate domains; and exact URI comparison for signed files.
6. **Endpoint publication (high):** direct `200` at `/.well-known/security.txt`; whether also to publish legacy `/security.txt`; redirect policy; behavior for traversal/acquisition and sub-sites; authentication bypass for the public endpoint; and prevention of HTML fallback responses.
7. **Response contract (medium):** exact `Content-Type`, UTF-8 encoding, LF versus CRLF output, final newline, cache headers, validators, and CDN invalidation.
8. **Extension preservation (medium):** permit arbitrary registered/unregistered extension lines, validate against the live IANA registry, and/or provide a safe advanced editor. Unknown fields must not break readers, but an authoring UI may still warn about malformed names or values.
9. **Comments/order fidelity (low to medium):** canonical generated order versus preserving author order and comments. Order has no protocol meaning but changes can invalidate an existing signature and create noisy diffs.
10. **Signing scope (high/security):** no signing; accept externally clear-signed text; or perform signing. In-product signing requires private-key storage, passphrase handling, permitted algorithms, key expiry/rotation, deterministic bytes, Canonical checks, and verification tests across current/deployed OpenPGP implementations.
11. **Validation depth (medium):** syntax-only versus deployment checks. DNS/TLS reachability, contact delivery, remote policy fetches, and key verification are operational checks beyond format generation and can introduce SSRF/privacy concerns.
12. **Update and registry policy (medium):** how the implementation learns about future IANA fields and official RFC errata without requiring a code release for every extension.

## 6. Recommended minimum acceptance baseline

A conforming first release should:

- publish unauthenticated HTTPS `200` content at `/.well-known/security.txt`;
- emit `text/plain; charset=utf-8` and valid UTF-8 with consistent line endings;
- require at least one valid URI-valued `Contact` and exactly one UTC `Expires` that is in the future and preferably less than one year away;
- enforce singleton versus repeatable fields as listed above;
- allow all current optional fields without making them mandatory;
- ignore or preserve syntactically valid unknown extension fields rather than assigning them invented semantics;
- treat comments and ordering as non-semantic;
- bound HTTP cache freshness by document expiry;
- keep OpenPGP signing optional, and if implemented, clear-sign the exact served representation, require matching `Canonical`, and verify the result with an independent conforming implementation; and
- test direct discovery, redirects if supported, wrong media type, malformed UTF-8, duplicate singletons, expired documents, proxy-derived Canonical values, caching, and signed line-ending/dash-escaping cases.

## Sources

Primary/high-trust sources retained:

- [RFC 9116 — A File Format to Aid in Security Vulnerability Disclosure](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html) — current defining standard.
- [Official RFC 9116 errata index](https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc9116) — authoritative location for verified/reported corrections; implementers should check status at implementation time.
- [IANA Security.txt Fields registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/security-txt-fields/security-txt-fields.xhtml) — live authoritative field registry.
- [securitytxt.org](https://securitytxt.org/) — first-party generator/authoring reference.
- [securitytxt/securitytxt.org](https://github.com/securitytxt/securitytxt.org) — first-party site source repository.
- [RFC 8615 — Well-Known Uniform Resource Identifiers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615.html) — well-known endpoint framework.
- [RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html) — current HTTP status, representation, and redirect semantics.
- [RFC 9111 — HTTP Caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html) — current caching rules.
- [RFC 2046 — Media Types](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2046.html) — `text/plain` representation rules.
- [RFC 3986 — URI Generic Syntax](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html) — URI-valued fields.
- [RFC 3339 — Date and Time on the Internet](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html) — expiry syntax.
- [RFC 5646 — Tags for Identifying Languages](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5646.html) — preferred-language tags.
- [RFC 4880 §7 — OpenPGP Cleartext Signature Framework](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7) — the framework normatively referenced by RFC 9116.
- [RFC 9580 — OpenPGP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) — current OpenPGP specification and migration context.

No blogs, vendor summaries, SEO pages, or third-party validators were used.

## Source gaps and residual uncertainty

- The official errata URL is included so implementation review can check the live disposition. This research environment could not retrieve live web content, so it did not independently attest the current count/status of RFC 9116 errata.
- For the same reason, the securitytxt.org generator inventory is intentionally capability-level rather than a control-by-control snapshot tied to a specific deployed commit. Before cloning its UX, inspect the live site and tagged/source revision for exact defaults, client-side transformations, accessibility, and download/signing behavior.
- Browser and crawler behavior varies beyond the RFC baseline, especially for redirects, cross-origin canonical copies, media-type parameters, and OpenPGP algorithm support. Interoperability tests against selected target consumers remain necessary.

See [RFC 9116 §3 and its ABNF](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3), [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html), [RFC 5646](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5646.html), and [RFC 3339 §5.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html#section-5.6).

The current standard fields are:

| Field | Required? | Multiplicity | Normative meaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `Contact` | **Required** | One or more | A URI describing how to report a vulnerability. Multiple contact methods may be published. Common schemes include `mailto:` and `https:`; accepting a URI is not the same as proving that the destination works. [RFC 9116 §2.5.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.3) |
| `Expires` | **Required** | Exactly one | UTC RFC 3339 date-time after which the file is stale and must not be treated as current. [RFC 9116 §2.5.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.5) |
| `Acknowledgments` | Optional | Zero or more | URI of a page recognizing security researchers. [RFC 9116 §2.5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.1) |
| `Canonical` | Optional unless clear-signed | Zero or more | URI identifying a canonical location of this same file; when the file is digitally signed, at least one `Canonical` field is required and must match the retrieval URI. [RFC 9116 §2.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.2) |
| `Encryption` | Optional | Zero or more | URI pointing to encryption keys or other information for encrypted communication. It is not itself an inline key. [RFC 9116 §2.5.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.4) |
| `Hiring` | Optional | Zero or more | URI for security-related job openings. [RFC 9116 §2.5.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.6) |
| `Policy` | Optional | Zero or more | URI of the service's security/disclosure policy. [RFC 9116 §2.5.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.7) |
| `Preferred-Languages` | Optional | At most one | One or more comma-separated BCP 47 language tags, in descending order of preference. [RFC 9116 §2.5.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.8) |

The registry is extensible. Consumers must ignore fields they do not recognize, and new standardized field names are added through the IANA registration policy rather than by silently assigning new semantics to an existing name. A control panel therefore should preserve or deliberately expose unknown extension lines if round-tripping is a goal; rejecting every unknown field would impair forward compatibility. See [RFC 9116 §3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3.1) and the live [IANA registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/security-txt-fields/security-txt-fields.xhtml).

### Expiry

`Expires` must represent a date and time in UTC using the RFC 3339 Internet date/time profile. RFC 9116 recommends a value less than one year into the future. A client must not use a file after its `Expires` time. This is document freshness, independent of HTTP cache freshness; both need to be honored. [RFC 9116 §2.5.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.5)

### Canonical

`Canonical` is not generally mandatory for an unsigned file. It becomes mandatory for a digitally signed file, where at least one value must match the URI used to retrieve that file. Multiple values allow the same content to identify more than one canonical deployment URI. This makes an automatically inferred value a product convenience, not a universal RFC default: virtual hosting, alternate ports, proxy headers, IDNs, and multi-site publication can make inference wrong. [RFC 9116 §2.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.2) and [§3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3)

### Comments and ordering

A comment line begins with `#`; comments and blank lines are permitted and do not define fields. Field order is not semantically significant. RFC 9116 gives a recommended human-readable ordering, but parsers cannot depend on it, and generators need not reorder user-authored content merely to be valid. Duplicate fields are valid only according to each field's multiplicity rules. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3)

## 2. HTTP discovery and representation

### Endpoint discovery

For an HTTP service, the standard location is the well-known URI `/.well-known/security.txt` on the authority being queried, and retrieval must use HTTPS. The legacy top-level `/security.txt` location may additionally be served for compatibility, but it is not a substitute for the well-known location. Well-known URI processing is governed by [RFC 8615](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615.html); security.txt's concrete discovery requirements are in [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3).

Scope follows the origin/authority being queried; a file found on one hostname should not silently be treated as authorization for unrelated hosts. The `Canonical` field identifies copies but does not turn arbitrary cross-origin content into an authoritative policy for every host. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3) and the origin model in [RFC 6454](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6454.html)

### Media type, charset, and line endings

The response media type is `text/plain` and the charset is UTF-8; the interoperable response header is `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`. Producers must emit valid UTF-8. Lines may end in either LF or CRLF under the security.txt grammar. A generated unsigned file should choose one style consistently; CRLF deserves special attention when OpenPGP cleartext signing because that framework canonicalizes line endings. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3), [`text/plain` in RFC 2046 §4.1.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2046.html#section-4.1.3), and [RFC 4880 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7)

### Status and redirects

Successful discovery is an HTTP `200 (OK)` representation at the well-known endpoint (possibly reached through a redirect). RFC 9116 clients are expected to handle redirects, but the RFC places security limits on redirect processing, including HTTPS destinations and a bounded redirect chain. A control panel should not assume that publishing a `3xx`, authentication challenge, HTML error page, or `200` fallback page containing non-security.txt content is equivalent to publishing a valid file. The current definitions of status-code and redirect semantics are in [RFC 9110 §§15.3.1 and 15.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.3.1), with security.txt-specific retrieval behavior in [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3).

Compatibility implication: serving the bytes directly at the well-known path is the least surprising baseline. If redirects are supported, the owner must decide whether to permit only same-origin redirects or also RFC-permitted cross-origin HTTPS redirects, and must test the framework/publisher so redirect loops and HTTP downgrades cannot occur.

### Caching

HTTP cache directives apply normally, but a cached representation cannot remain semantically current beyond its `Expires` field. The publisher should set cache freshness so it ends no later than document expiry and should allow a promptly updated contact or policy to propagate. Conversely, the document's `Expires` value does not itself replace HTTP `Cache-Control` or HTTP cache validation. See [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3) and the current HTTP caching specification, [RFC 9111](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html).

A practical generator can compute `max-age <= Expires - now`, but that computation is convenience behavior, not a new security.txt field requirement. Product policy still has to address shared caches/CDNs, clock skew, revalidation (`ETag`/`Last-Modified`), emergency updates, and whether an expired configured document is served with warnings, rejected, or automatically disabled.

## 3. OpenPGP clear-signing

RFC 9116 permits, but does not require, the entire security.txt file to be digitally signed using the OpenPGP cleartext signature framework. This is a clear-signed document (`BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE`, `Hash` header, clear text, and armored signature), not an attached signature field and not merely an `Encryption` URI. When signed, `Canonical` is mandatory and at least one canonical URI must match the URI from which the signed file was retrieved. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3) and [RFC 4880 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7)

Cleartext signing has byte-level constraints: trailing spaces/tabs are ignored for signature calculation, line endings are canonicalized to CRLF for hashing, and lines beginning with a hyphen are dash-escaped in the armored cleartext form. Implementations should delegate this to a conforming OpenPGP library rather than reproduce it with ad hoc string transformations. [RFC 4880 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7)

RFC 4880 was obsoleted by the current OpenPGP specification, [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html), but RFC 9116's normative reference and deployed security.txt tooling use the cleartext-signature framework terminology established by RFC 4880. This creates an explicit compatibility decision: select library/key/signature profiles that satisfy current OpenPGP security guidance while remaining verifiable by deployed security.txt consumers. The product also needs a key custody and rotation model; RFC conformance alone does not make server-side storage of a private signing key safe. [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) and [RFC 9116 references](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#name-normative-references)

## 4. securitytxt.org authoring/generation inventory

[securitytxt.org](https://securitytxt.org/) is the first-party project site associated with the standard and exposes an interactive authoring generator. Its source repository is published as [`securitytxt/securitytxt.org`](https://github.com/securitytxt/securitytxt.org). These are useful UX references, not a second standards authority.

The site's authoring surface covers the registered baseline fields: required contact and expiry, plus acknowledgments, canonical location, encryption information, hiring, policy, and preferred languages. It guides a user through values and emits security.txt text suitable for copying/downloading. Any default expiry, field ordering, repeat/add controls, URI widgets, language picker, examples, or automatic formatting supplied by that UI are generator conveniences; validity and multiplicity remain controlled by RFC 9116 and IANA. See the live [generator](https://securitytxt.org/) and its [first-party source](https://github.com/securitytxt/securitytxt.org).

Not in scope here: the site's facility for validating an arbitrary remote site. This baseline inventories authoring/generation only and does not recommend proxying, reproducing, or depending on its remote validator.

A product should not infer from the site's UI that it may:

- omit either `Contact` or `Expires`;
- force optional fields to be present;
- reject registered future extensions merely because no widget exists;
- treat a default expiry interval as normative;
- assume generated output is deployed at the URL declared by `Canonical`;
- claim that a generated contact, URL, encryption key, or signature has been operationally verified; or
- call an unsigned generated file non-conforming, since signing is optional.

## 5. Concrete owner decisions

The following choices are not completely determined by the RFC and should be made explicitly before implementation:

1. **Authoring model (high product impact):** structured fields only, raw text only, or a hybrid. A structured-only model is simpler but needs a strategy for comments, blank lines, and unknown IANA extension fields to avoid lossy round trips.
2. **Multiplicity UX (medium):** repeatable controls for `Contact`, `Acknowledgments`, `Canonical`, `Encryption`, `Hiring`, and `Policy`; singleton enforcement for `Expires` and `Preferred-Languages`; and whether duplicate singletons are hard errors at save time.
3. **URI schemes (medium):** whether to accept every syntactically valid URI allowed by the RFC or constrain schemes for safety/UX. `mailto:` and HTTPS are important; a restrictive allowlist is a product policy and could exclude legitimate registered URI schemes.
4. **Expiry lifecycle (high):** default interval (while keeping it under the RFC's recommended one-year horizon), warning cadence, renewal flow, clock source, and behavior when configured content expires. Silent perpetual auto-extension undermines the purpose of explicit expiry.
5. **Canonical derivation (high):** manual values versus proxy-aware inference; behavior across virtual hosts, sites, ports, aliases, and alternate domains; and exact URI comparison for signed files.
6. **Endpoint publication (high):** direct `200` at `/.well-known/security.txt`; whether also to publish legacy `/security.txt`; redirect policy; behavior for traversal/acquisition and sub-sites; authentication bypass for the public endpoint; and prevention of HTML fallback responses.
7. **Response contract (medium):** exact `Content-Type`, UTF-8 encoding, LF versus CRLF output, final newline, cache headers, validators, and CDN invalidation.
8. **Extension preservation (medium):** permit arbitrary registered/unregistered extension lines, validate against the live IANA registry, and/or provide a safe advanced editor. Unknown fields must not break readers, but an authoring UI may still warn about malformed names or values.
9. **Comments/order fidelity (low to medium):** canonical generated order versus preserving author order and comments. Order has no protocol meaning but changes can invalidate an existing signature and create noisy diffs.
10. **Signing scope (high/security):** no signing; accept externally clear-signed text; or perform signing. In-product signing requires private-key storage, passphrase handling, permitted algorithms, key expiry/rotation, deterministic bytes, Canonical checks, and verification tests across current/deployed OpenPGP implementations.
11. **Validation depth (medium):** syntax-only versus deployment checks. DNS/TLS reachability, contact delivery, remote policy fetches, and key verification are operational checks beyond format generation and can introduce SSRF/privacy concerns.
12. **Update and registry policy (medium):** how the implementation learns about future IANA fields and official RFC errata without requiring a code release for every extension.

## 6. Recommended minimum acceptance baseline

A conforming first release should:

- publish unauthenticated HTTPS `200` content at `/.well-known/security.txt`;
- emit `text/plain; charset=utf-8` and valid UTF-8 with consistent line endings;
- require at least one valid URI-valued `Contact` and exactly one UTC `Expires` that is in the future and preferably less than one year away;
- enforce singleton versus repeatable fields as listed above;
- allow all current optional fields without making them mandatory;
- ignore or preserve syntactically valid unknown extension fields rather than assigning them invented semantics;
- treat comments and ordering as non-semantic;
- bound HTTP cache freshness by document expiry;
- keep OpenPGP signing optional, and if implemented, clear-sign the exact served representation, require matching `Canonical`, and verify the result with an independent conforming implementation; and
- test direct discovery, redirects if supported, wrong media type, malformed UTF-8, duplicate singletons, expired documents, proxy-derived Canonical values, caching, and signed line-ending/dash-escaping cases.

## Sources

Primary/high-trust sources retained:

- [RFC 9116 — A File Format to Aid in Security Vulnerability Disclosure](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html) — current defining standard.
- [Official RFC 9116 errata index](https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc9116) — authoritative location for verified/reported corrections; implementers should check status at implementation time.
- [IANA Security.txt Fields registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/security-txt-fields/security-txt-fields.xhtml) — live authoritative field registry.
- [securitytxt.org](https://securitytxt.org/) — first-party generator/authoring reference.
- [securitytxt/securitytxt.org](https://github.com/securitytxt/securitytxt.org) — first-party site source repository.
- [RFC 8615 — Well-Known Uniform Resource Identifiers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615.html) — well-known endpoint framework.
- [RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html) — current HTTP status, representation, and redirect semantics.
- [RFC 9111 — HTTP Caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html) — current caching rules.
- [RFC 2046 — Media Types](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2046.html) — `text/plain` representation rules.
- [RFC 3986 — URI Generic Syntax](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html) — URI-valued fields.
- [RFC 3339 — Date and Time on the Internet](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html) — expiry syntax.
- [RFC 5646 — Tags for Identifying Languages](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5646.html) — preferred-language tags.
- [RFC 4880 §7 — OpenPGP Cleartext Signature Framework](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4880.html#section-7) — the framework normatively referenced by RFC 9116.
- [RFC 9580 — OpenPGP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) — current OpenPGP specification and migration context.

No blogs, vendor summaries, SEO pages, or third-party validators were used.

## Source gaps and residual uncertainty

- The official errata URL is included so implementation review can check the live disposition. This research environment could not retrieve live web content, so it did not independently attest the current count/status of RFC 9116 errata.
- For the same reason, the securitytxt.org generator inventory is intentionally capability-level rather than a control-by-control snapshot tied to a specific deployed commit. Before cloning its UX, inspect the live site and tagged/source revision for exact defaults, client-side transformations, accessibility, and download/signing behavior.
- Browser and crawler behavior varies beyond the RFC baseline, especially for redirects, cross-origin canonical copies, media-type parameters, and OpenPGP algorithm support. Interoperability tests against selected target consumers remain necessary.

# security.txt standards baseline

Research date: 2026-03-10

## Executive baseline

The current security.txt standard is [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html), which obsoletes RFC 2142's narrower treatment of a security contact. For an HTTP service, the interoperable baseline is a UTF-8 plain-text document at `https://<authority>/.well-known/security.txt` containing one or more `Contact` fields and exactly one unexpired `Expires` field. The standard makes all other currently registered fields optional. Product behavior should be based on RFC 9116 and the live [IANA Security.txt Fields registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/security-txt-fields/security-txt-fields.xhtml), not on which controls happen to appear in the securitytxt.org generator.

Normative words below describe RFC requirements only where the RFC uses them. Generator behavior is called out separately as convenience behavior.

## 1. Syntax, fields, and multiplicity

RFC 9116 defines a line-oriented format. A field line consists of a registered field name, `:`, one space, and its value; field names use letters, digits, and hyphens. Field names are case-insensitive, while values retain the semantics of their field. Blank lines and comment lines are also allowed. URI-valued fields use URI syntax; `Preferred-Languages` is a comma-separated list of language tags; `Expires` is an RFC 3339 date-time constrained as described below. See [RFC 9116 §3 and its ABNF](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3), [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.html), [RFC 5646](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5646.html), and [RFC 3339 §5.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339.html#section-5.6).

The current standard fields are:

| Field | Required? | Multiplicity | Normative meaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `Contact` | **Required** | One or more | A URI describing how to report a vulnerability. Multiple contact methods may be published. Common schemes include `mailto:` and `https:`; accepting a URI is not the same as proving that the destination works. [RFC 9116 §2.5.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.3) |
| `Expires` | **Required** | Exactly one | UTC RFC 3339 date-time after which the file is stale and must not be treated as current. [RFC 9116 §2.5.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.5) |
| `Acknowledgments` | Optional | Zero or more | URI of a page recognizing security researchers. [RFC 9116 §2.5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.1) |
| `Canonical` | Optional unless clear-signed | Zero or more | URI identifying a canonical location of this same file; when the file is digitally signed, at least one `Canonical` field is required and must match the retrieval URI. [RFC 9116 §2.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.2) |
| `Encryption` | Optional | Zero or more | URI pointing to encryption keys or other information for encrypted communication. It is not itself an inline key. [RFC 9116 §2.5.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.4) |
| `Hiring` | Optional | Zero or more | URI for security-related job openings. [RFC 9116 §2.5.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.6) |
| `Policy` | Optional | Zero or more | URI of the service's security/disclosure policy. [RFC 9116 §2.5.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.7) |
| `Preferred-Languages` | Optional | At most one | One or more comma-separated BCP 47 language tags, in descending order of preference. [RFC 9116 §2.5.8](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.8) |

The registry is extensible. Consumers must ignore fields they do not recognize, and new standardized field names are added through the IANA registration policy rather than by silently assigning new semantics to an existing name. A control panel therefore should preserve or deliberately expose unknown extension lines if round-tripping is a goal; rejecting every unknown field would impair forward compatibility. See [RFC 9116 §3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3.1) and the live [IANA registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/security-txt-fields/security-txt-fields.xhtml).

### Expiry

`Expires` must represent a date and time in UTC using the RFC 3339 Internet date/time profile. RFC 9116 recommends a value less than one year into the future. A client must not use a file after its `Expires` time. This is document freshness, independent of HTTP cache freshness; both need to be honored. [RFC 9116 §2.5.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.5)

### Canonical

`Canonical` is not generally mandatory for an unsigned file. It becomes mandatory for a digitally signed file, where at least one value must match the URI used to retrieve that file. Multiple values allow the same content to identify more than one canonical deployment URI. This makes an automatically inferred value a product convenience, not a universal RFC default: virtual hosting, alternate ports, proxy headers, IDNs, and multi-site publication can make inference wrong. [RFC 9116 §2.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-2.5.2) and [§3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3)

### Comments and ordering

A comment line begins with `#`; comments and blank lines are permitted and do not define fields. Field order is not semantically significant. RFC 9116 gives a recommended human-readable ordering, but parsers cannot depend on it, and generators need not reorder user-authored content merely to be valid. Duplicate fields are valid only according to each field's multiplicity rules. [RFC 9116 §3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html#section-3)

- OpenPGP signing is optional, but signed files require a matching `Canonical`.
